title: Pipeline Safety: Amendments to Liquefied Natural Gas Facilities
content: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration 49 CFR Parts 191 and 193 [Docket No. PHMSA-2019-0091] RIN 2137-AF45 Pipeline Safety: Amendments to Liquefied Natural Gas Facilities ACTION: Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM). AGENCY: Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), Department of Transportation (DOT). SUMMARY: PHMSA proposes updating its regulations for liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities to incorporate by reference the most recent industry safety standards and to make other changes to account for more than two decades of improvements and technological advancements. This rulemaking also responds to congressional mandates directing PHMSA to integrate risk-based regulatory approaches for certain LNG facilities. DATES: Comments on this NPRM must be submitted by January 4, 2027. A public meeting of PHMSA's statutory advisory committees will be held on a date to be announced in the Federal Register . ADDRESSES: Submit comments by any of the following methods, identifying docket number PHMSA-2019-0091 at the top of the first page: • On https://www.regulations.gov, follow instructions to “submit a comment.” • By mail or hand delivery to Docket Management System, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001. Hand delivery is available to this address between 9:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday (except Federal holidays). Include two copies if submitting by mail and include a self-addressed and stamped postcard to receive confirmation of receipt. Comments may be viewed at https://www.regulations.gov/docket/PHMSA-2019-0091. Comments are posted without changes or edits, including any personal information provided. DOT's privacy statement can be reviewed at https://www.dot.gov/privacy. A plain language summary of the proposed rule is also available in section I.B. that is placed on the rulemaking docket, pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4). Confidential Business Information (CBI): You may designate a comment as CBI if your comment contains commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private and that you actually treat as private by sending to Brianna Wilson, at the contact information listed below, the following: (1) the original document with each page containing CBI marked as “confidential;” (2) a redacted copy with the CBI deleted; and (3) an explanation of why the information you are submitting is CBI. See 49 CFR 190.343. Any comment not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket. FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Brianna Wilson, Standards and Rulemaking Division, by phone at (771) 215-0969 or by email at brianna.wilson@dot.gov. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Table of Contents I. Executive Summary II. Background III. Section-by-Section Discussion of the Proposed Changes in Part 191 IV. Section-by-Section Discussion of the Proposed Changes in Part 193 V. Regulatory Analyses and Notices I. Executive Summary A. Purpose and Scope of the Regulatory Action PHMSA has been regulating the safety of LNG facilities for more than five decades. When PHMSA issued the first Federal safety standards in 1970, the U.S. LNG industry comprised mostly relatively small “peak-shaving” facilities used to liquefy and store natural gas for delivery to local markets during times of peak demand. The handful of large-scale LNG facilities at that time were primarily built to import natural gas for domestic consumption. The U.S. LNG industry did not have a significant role as an exporter of natural gas. Market conditions have changed dramatically since the 1970s. U.S. natural gas production has increased significantly, particularly in the past two decades as technological advancements in the oil and gas industry have led to the development of energy resources from the Nation's shale plays. Domestic natural gas demand has continued to grow, and an increasing number of U.S.-based facilities are exporting LNG to foreign markets. These changes have created a need for the construction of new LNG facilities and for the expansion of existing LNG facilities. Modern operational and maintenance practices within the LNG industry are considerably more sophisticated and robust, reflecting many thousands of hours of experience since the 1970s. New technologies have emerged, such as “membrane” tanks (which employ a thin cryogenic steel inner liner with a load-bearing, concrete outer tank—an approach offering improved storage capacity, reduced material costs, and faster construction schedules than earlier LNG storage tank designs) and pipe-in-pipe (PIP) transfer systems (which provide enhanced containment of releases from cryogenic piping). PHMSA's oversight of the LNG industry has not kept pace with these dramatic changes. PHMSA's LNG regulations are largely based on the 2001 edition of an industry standard, NFPA 59A, Standard for the Production, Storage, and Handling of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG), and have not been updated since 2006. NFPA 59A-2001 is now seven editions out of date, and multiple stakeholders have called on PHMSA to update its regulations to account for the latest practices in the siting, design, construction, operation, and maintenance of LNG facilities. For example, in the Protecting our Infrastructure of Pipelines and Enhancing Safety Act of 2016 (PIPES Act of 2016), Congress directed PHMSA to develop regulations for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities, an issue specifically addressed in the more recent editions of NFPA 59A. 1 In the Protecting our Infrastructure of Pipelines and Enhancing Safety Act of 2020 (PIPES Act of 2020), Congress directed PHMSA to develop alternative, risk-based operations and maintenance requirements for large-scale LNG facilities, an approach consistent with modern regulatory frameworks that apply in other industries. 2 The Government Accountability Office (GAO) has also advised PHMSA to update its regulations to align better with current editions of consensus industry standards. 3 1 PIPES Act of 2016, Public Law 114-183 (June 22, 2016). 2 PIPES Act of 2020, Public Law 116-260 (Dec. 27, 2020). 3 GAO, Natural Gas Exports: Updated Guidance and Regulations Could Improve Facility Permitting Processes (Aug. 6, 2020) (GAO Report). To address these concerns, PHMSA proposes a comprehensive revision to its safety standards for LNG facilities. The proposed amendments would enhance public safety by incorporating the latest consensus industry standards for the siting, design, construction, operation, and maintenance of LNG facilities. These changes will promote the use of new technologies, reduce unnecessary barriers to investment, and provide regulatory certainty for interested stakeholders. PHMSA's proposals will also address outstanding Congressional mandates and GAO recommendations and advance the President's commitments to unleashing American energy, sustaining U.S. defense operations, and ensuring the energy security of the U.S. and its allies. B. Summary of the Major Regulatory Provisions Below is a high-level summary of the most substantial changes proposed in this document. This NPRM discusses each change in more detail in the “Section-by-Section Discussion of the Proposed Changes.” 1. Calibrating Reporting Requirements to Public Safety Risks PHMSA proposes to amend the reporting requirements for safety-related conditions and incidents. First, PHMSA proposes to clarify that operators of LNG facilities must report safety-related conditions and incidents during initial startup. This clarification would help ensure that operators are reporting incidents and safety-related conditions that occur at the earliest phase in the operational lifetime of an LNG facility, which is critical in determining its long-term integrity. PHMSA also proposes to broaden the definition of incidents and safety-related conditions to encompass hazardous fluids beyond LNG alone; this proposed change will improve risk mitigation and incident response by focusing on the various materials involved in gas processing activities at LNG facilities. Second, PHMSA proposes to revise the incident and annual report forms to eliminate content with little or no safety value, and to update the operator identification number (OPID) and annual report forms to accommodate the new requirements for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities in subpart D. 2. Incorporation by Reference Updated Editions of Leading Industry Standards PHMSA proposes to incorporate by reference the 2026 edition of NFPA 59A. 4 PHMSA currently incorporates the 2001 edition of NFPA 59A for most purposes. Incorporating the 2026 edition is consistent with PHMSA's longstanding practice of integrating NFPA 59A as a key component of its regulations for LNG facilities. As part of that process, PHMSA proposes to redesignate or to remove certain duplicative or unnecessary regulatory requirements and to modify or to supplement certain provisions in NFPA 59A-2026 ( e.g., design wind resistance of certain LNG facilities; design spill assumptions in hazard modeling) to accommodate significant public safety risks or to facilitate implementation. 4 National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), 59A-2026 Standard for the Production, Storage, and Handling of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) (Dec. 9, 2025) (NFPA 59A-2026). Incorporating NFPA 59A-2026 would enhance the requirements for the siting, design, installation, construction, operations, and maintenance of LNG facilities and align PHMSA's regulations with the latest safety-enhancing practices and technologies. It would also reduce certain compliance costs by allowing LNG operators to use those practices and technologies without obtaining special permits or waivers and address outstanding Congressional mandates and GAO recommendations. 3. Improved Alignment Between Facility Siting Requirements and Safety Risks PHMSA proposes to incorporate by reference the traditional, prescriptive siting requirements in chapter 5 of NFPA 59A-2026. Incorporating chapter 5 would expand the universe of hazards operators must evaluate to comply with the part 193, subpart B siting requirements, ensuring that those analyses are consistent with current knowledge of the public safety risks posed by releases of hazardous fluids from LNG facilities. PHMSA also proposes to incorporate the new risk-based siting requirements in chapter 19 ( Performance-Based LNG Plant Siting Using Quantitative Risk Analysis (QRA) ) of NFPA 59A-2026. PHMSA expects that the QRA-based approach will improve facility safety by allowing a more sophisticated understanding of public safety risks, enhancing the allocation of resources, and incentivizing deployment of innovative operational practices and technology. PHMSA expects that improved flexibility regarding LNG facility siting and internal layout under the QRA-based approach could enable investment in additional capacity at existing locations. 4. Introduction of Targeted Requirements for Permanent, Small-Scale LNG Facilities PHMSA proposes to establish requirements for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities by incorporating chapter 17 of NFPA 59A-2026 by reference into a new subpart D. Permanent, small-scale LNG facilities entail lower risks to public safety and the environment than larger LNG facilities, primarily due to their distinguishable liquefaction processes, lower liquefaction capacity, and smaller LNG storage volumes, and should be regulated accordingly. Incorporating the chapter 17 requirements would also address the rulemaking mandate in section 27(b) of the PIPES Act of 2016 for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities. 5. Integration of an Alternative, Risk-based Operations and Maintenance Framework Consistent with section 110 of the PIPES Act of 2020, PHMSA proposes to adopt an alternative, risk-based operations and maintenance (O&M) program for FERC-jurisdictional LNG facilities in a new subpart F. The risk-based O&M alternative would be a structured program with procedures developed and implemented to identify, to evaluate, and to mitigate or to eliminate hazards and the resulting risks. Operators employing this approach would have flexibility to tailor a risk-based approach to the specific risks from their facilities. Operators electing to use the risk-based O&M alternative would be required to submit an implementation plan specifying a timeline for integration of program elements. C. Costs and Benefits PHMSA estimates the annualized cost savings from the proposed rule to be approximately $98 million (discounted at three percent). PHMSA notes that some of the new compliance costs and many of the cost savings of the proposed rule could not be quantified based on the available data. PHMSA anticipates significant unquantified safety benefits would result from adopting the safety-enhancing elements of NFPA 59A-2026, as supplemented and qualified by other proposed part 193 amendments. Because LNG facilities are complex systems whose failure generally involves multiple “but for” causes, PHMSA was not able to quantify a reduction in incident risk pursuant to the proposed rule. Other unquantified benefits include increased flexibility for LNG facility siting under the QRA-based approach in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 19, increased regulatory flexibility for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities subject to the requirements in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 17, and the use of new technologies, such as membrane tanks, single-walled ASME (American Society of Mechanical Engineers) containers, and PIP systems, which PHMSA was not able to quantify due to uncertainty around potential uptake of the proposed flexibilities. The preliminary regulatory impact analysis (PRIA) provided in the docket for this rulemaking includes additional information about the costs, benefits, and other impacts of the proposed rule. The PRIA's quantification of costs and benefits reflects assumptions and estimates based on the information and data available. PHMSA requests information and data from the public regarding the PRIA's evaluation of expected costs and benefits of its proposed requirements. PHMSA has preliminarily determined that, notwithstanding the uncertainties and data limitations discussed in the PRIA, the proposals in the NPRM would be justified by their corresponding compliance costs savings, enhanced regulatory flexibility, or improved public safety benefits. II. Background A. LNG as an Energy Source, Industry Growth, and Regulatory Safety 1. LNG as an Energy Source Natural gas is vital to the energy and economic security of the United States and its allies abroad, serving as an economic driver and essential fuel source for residential, commercial, and industrial purposes. Total annual U.S. natural gas consumption has increased from 5.0 Tcf in 1949 to 33.5 Tcf in 2025. 5 Global natural gas consumption similarly is expected to grow from 152.9 Tcf to 194.3 Tcf by 2050 due to increasing demand in emerging markets and developing economies. 6 Domestic U.S. and international demand for natural gas has made it an important driver of the U.S. economy; a smaller U.S. natural gas sector in 2018 contributed over 3.4 million jobs and $408 billion to U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP). 7 5 U.S. Energy Info. Admin. (EIA), Natural Gas: U.S Gas Total Consumption, available at: https://www.eia.gov/dnav/ng/hist/n9140us2a.htm (last visited Apr. 23, 2026). 6 EIA, International Energy Outlook 2023 Table: World Natural Gas Consumption by Region, available at: https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/aeo/data/browser/#/?id=6-IEO2023&region=0-0&cases=Reference&start=2020&end=2050&f=A&linechart=Reference-d230822.21-6-IEO2023&map=&ctype=linechart&sourcekey=0. 7 Am. Gas Ass'n (AGA), Benefits to the Economy through the Direct Use of Natural Gas (July 9, 2020), available at: https://www.aga.org/research-policy/resource-library/benefits-to-the-economy-through-the-direct-use-of-natural-gas/. Increased reliance on natural gas from a variety of applications is contributing to this growing demand. First, natural gas is a critical source of electric power generation capacity and grid stability. In addition to providing dispatchable electricity, natural gas electric power generation also supplies grid attributes ( e.g., inertia) increasingly vital to grid stability as more intermittent renewable energy generation capacity joins the grid and baseload coal and nuclear plants retire. Second, natural gas is essential for many industrial feedstock and process heat applications, as well as commercial and residential heating and cooking purposes. Third, natural gas is an increasingly vital fuel source in the transportation sector, powering maritime vessels ( i.e., marine bunkering), fueling truck fleets, and providing an alternative gas supply during pipeline testing activities. But many regions—both within the United States and the wider world—do not have reliable access to natural gas. Some regions are far-removed from natural gas supply reservoirs; others have limited pipeline infrastructure enabling transportation of natural gas in gaseous form or are vulnerable to supply interruptions on natural gas pipelines. Reliable natural gas supply in such circumstances may turn on access to LNG—natural gas that has been cooled to low temperatures (minus 260 °F or minus 162 °C) and converted to a liquid state. This conversion process, known as liquefaction, reduces the volume of natural gas to approximately 1/600th of its volume in a gaseous state. The reduction in volume makes LNG efficient for transportation and storage purposes in areas with limited natural gas resources or limited pipeline supply of natural gas. Prior to liquefaction, the natural gas must be treated (pre-treatment) to remove impurities and extract heavy hydrocarbons (extraction). The pre-treatment, hydrocarbon extraction, and liquefaction processes may involve a number of hazardous fluids—including materials that are flammable ( e.g., methane, ethane, ethylene, propane, butane, pentane, other heavy hydrocarbons including aromatic hydrocarbons, hydrogen sulfide, and anhydrous ammonia); toxic ( e.g., aromatic hydrocarbons, hydrogen sulfide, and anhydrous ammonia); and corrosive ( e.g., anhydrous ammonia, amine solution, and aromatic hydrocarbons). Such hazardous materials can be present in either gaseous or liquid form at different stages of these processes. Larger LNG facilities, such as import or export terminals, will typically employ more complex liquefaction processes (and different, and larger quantities of, hazardous fluids) than smaller LNG facilities, such as peak shavers and mobile and temporary facilities. After liquefaction, LNG is stored and transported in specialized tanks that are insulated and refrigerated to maintain low temperatures. When needed for use, LNG undergoes a regasification process in which it is warmed and converted back into its gaseous state. The vaporized natural gas can then be injected into a pipeline system for distribution or used as fuel for natural gas-operated equipment. The flexibility arising from the transportation and storage of LNG has made it a vital element in natural gas supply infrastructures around the world. Within the United States, LNG peak shaving facilities provide local customers with access to natural gas during times of peak demand. There is also increasing interest in developing small-scale, mobile, or temporary LNG facilities to support novel applications ( e.g., ensuring continuity of power to data centers and for industrial applications). And U.S. LNG export facilities are a critical energy resource for a variety of countries—including strategic U.S. allies in Asia and Europe—which either have limited native energy resources, desires to diversify their energy portfolios, or plans to transition away from coal for electric power and process heat generation. Recent supply disruptions of LNG exports from international LNG suppliers like Qatar have also underscored the unique value of U.S. LNG exports to the energy security of America's trading partners. 2. Growth and Increasing Domestic and International Significance of the U.S. LNG Industry The U.S. LNG industry has undergone significant changes in the two decades since PHMSA last amended its part 193 regulations. The design and configuration of the 117 regulated LNG facilities in service at that time reflected the more limited role of natural gas within the domestic U.S. economy and consisted mostly of the following: • Peak-shaving plants designed to store surplus natural gas for use during high demand periods, such as summer and winter. Peak-shaving plants ensure reliability by liquefying and storing natural gas when demand is low and re-gasifying and distributing natural gas when demand is high. Natural gas shortages in the 1970s drove a wave of construction of peak-shaving plants. Operators began slowly retiring those plants in subsequent decades. The number of peak-shaving plants decreased from 75 in 2006 to 67 in 2018. • Satellite plants serving peak-shaving purposes but lacking the processing equipment required to convert natural gas to LNG. Specially equipped trucks (or tanks transported on rail flatcars) deliver LNG to satellite plants, where the LNG is stored and later re-gasified and injected into natural gas distribution systems to meet demand. In 2006, there were 23 satellite plants. • Mobile and temporary LNG plants designed to be easily movable rather than permanent structures. Mobile LNG plants, such as skid-mounted or trailer-mounted units, can be relocated as needed. Temporary LNG plants are used for short-term applications, providing supply during planned construction and maintenance activities or to meet unanticipated demand. Mobile and temporary LNG plants are compact and often located near end users to minimize transportation costs and enhance accessibility. In 2006, there were nine mobile and temporary facilities. • Large-scale terminals for importing LNG for domestic use, exporting LNG to foreign markets, or both. In 2006, the United States was a net importer of natural gas; there were four import terminals and one export terminal representing an aggregate 4.877 Bcf/d vaporization capacity. These terminals played a relatively small role in the U.S. and global energy economy in 2006. The shale gas revolution has fundamentally reshaped domestic and international energy markets over the past two decades. Newly abundant natural gas supplies have resulted in a rapid expansion of natural gas power generation capacity and industrial and commercial applications within the United States—a trend that is expected to accelerate due to onshoring of industrial capacity and skyrocketing demand for continuous electric generation capacity supporting super intelligence and data centers. 8 The number of part 193-regulated U.S. LNG facilities has increased in response to these recent market developments. As of 2025, there are 69 peak shaving plants, many of which are larger, and more complex, than the smaller plants typical in 2006. The number of other PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG plants has increased as well: in 2004, there were 22 satellite plants, 8 mobile or temporary facilities, and 4 import terminals (representing 4.877 Bcf/d import capacity); in 2025 there were 32 satellite plants, 43 mobile or temporary facilities, and 9 import terminals (representing 14.934 Bcf/d import capacity). Abundant natural gas supplies have also resulted in proliferation of so-called “small-scale” applications of LNG catering to niche markets, including off-grid power generation, localized peak-shaving, industrial equipment usage (such as oil and gas drilling equipment), and transportation fuels for vehicles, rail, or maritime use. 9 8 See Sturgeon (Xcel) & Hummel (Chart Industries), Transcript of Oct. 2025 Public Meeting, Docket ID PHMSA-2019-0091-7624, at 67:12-70:20, 72:20-77:16 (Oct. 25, 2025). 9 See Hummel (Chart Industries), Transcript of Oct. 2025 Public Meeting, Docket ID PHMSA-2019-0091-7624, at 72:20-77:16 (Oct. 25, 2025); Christa Marshall, Data Centers Increasingly Turn to Off-Grid Gas, EE News (Feb. 5, 2026). But the most significant change since 2006 has been the emergence of enormous U.S. natural gas export capacity. The United States now boasts eight operational, PHMSA-jurisdictional export terminals providing ca. 17.0 Bcf/d of capacity. Sixteen additional projects (providing an additional ca. 31.28 Bcf/d capacity) either are in construction or are expected to begin construction in the near future. 10 And the United States—a net importer of natural gas in 2006—exported approximately 15.1 Bcf/d of LNG in 2024, making it the world's largest LNG exporter, responsible for roughly 21 percent of worldwide LNG supply. 10 PHMSA, Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) Annual Data—2010 to Present, available at: https://www.phmsa.dot.gov/data-and-statistics/pipeline/gas-distribution-gas-gathering-gas-transmission-hazardous-liquids (last visited Apr. 14, 2026); FERC, U.S. LNG Export Terminals—Existing, Approved Not Yet Built, and Proposed, available at: https://www.ferc.gov/media/us-lng-export-terminals-existing-approved-not-yet-built-and-proposed (last visited Apr. 14, 2026). LNG exports have become critical to U.S. economic prosperity and national security. A 2026 study predicts that through 2040 U.S. LNG exports will contribute an aggregate of around $1.4 trillion to U.S. GDP, more than $2.9 trillion in total revenues for U.S. businesses, $206 billion in Federal and State tax revenues, and more than $630 billion in labor income. The industry will support an average of over a half-million U.S. jobs annually. 11 U.S. LNG exports also reduce trade deficits with economic competitors and have become a focal point for U.S. policymakers in recent tariff negotiations with U.S. trading partners. 12 U.S. LNG exports are a vital form of support for key U.S. allies as well. Europe and Asia were the top destinations for U.S. LNG exports in 2025. 13 Japan alone imported 222.9 Bcf of U.S. LNG in 2025, roughly 4.0 percent of the U.S. LNG exports for 2025. The Netherlands imported 645.8 Bcf of U.S. LNG in 2025, the most of any country and roughly 11.7 percent of U.S. LNG exports that year. 14 Exports to Europe increased following Russia's invasion of Ukraine; in 2022, Europe received 69 percent of all LNG exports from the United States, up from 34 percent in 2021. From January through November 2025, Europe received 68 percent of U.S.-origin volumes. 15 11 S&P Global, Price and Economic Impacts of an Accelerating Export Industry: U.S. LNG Impact Study—Phase 4 (July 2026). 12 Reuters, U.S. LNG Producers Climb as EU Agrees to $750 Billion in Energy Purchases (July 28, 2025), available at: https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/us-lng-producers-climb-eu-agrees-750-billion-energy-purchases-2025-07-28/. 13 EIA, Today in Energy: U.S. Natural Gas Exports to Grow Nearly 30% by 2027 as LNG Facilities Ramp Up (Apr. 16, 2026), available at: https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67484. 14 EIA, U.S. Natural Gas Exports and Re-Exports by Country, available at: https://www.eia.gov/dnav/ng/NG_MOVE_EXPC_S1_A.htm (last visited Apr. 22, 2026). 15 EIA, Today in Energy: Ten Years After First Sabine Pass Cargo, U.S. LNG Exports are Still on the Rise (Feb. 24, 2026), available at: https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67224. 3. The Regulatory Framework and Industry Efforts To Ensure LNG Facility Safety Multiple Federal agencies play a role in ensuring the safety of onshore LNG facilities. 16 These agencies exercise their respective authorities through a variety of administrative tools—including implementing regulations, guidance, orders, and enforcement actions—that can govern different phases of the lifecycle (including authorization, construction, and operations) of LNG facilities. The States also have a role in administering the Federal safety framework for intrastate LNG facilities. Industry, too, has pursued continuous safety improvement, developing voluntary (but widely adopted) consensus and industry codes, standards, recommended practices, guidelines reflecting safety-enhancing best practices, and technological advances that have outpaced the development of Federal safety regulatory regimes. These mutually reinforcing approaches have yielded a strong historical safety record for all PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG facilities. 16 PHMSA has not attempted to identify here the entire universe of Federal agencies whose regulatory schemes could touch on the diverse activities of PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG facilities but instead focused on those playing the most prominent role in their safety regulation. a. The Regulatory Framework Ensuring Safety Guardrails for Federal agencies' exercise of their respective regulatory authorities over the safety of LNG facilities are set forth in a series of interagency agreements and memoranda of understanding. Noteworthy among those interagency efforts are: a 2004 Interagency Agreement between PHMSA, FERC, and the USCG governing waterfront LNG facilities (typically FERC-jurisdictional import and export facilities); 17 a 2018 Memorandum of Understanding between FERC and PHMSA regarding PHMSA's role in FERC's environmental analyses supporting LNG facility certificate applications; 18 and a 2020 Annex to a 2004 Memorandum of Understanding between DOT and DHS outlining the respective roles of PHMSA and the DHS agencies (including TSA, USCG, and CISA) regarding the physical and cybersecurity of PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG facilities. 19 17 Interagency Agreement Among the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, United States Coast Guard, and Research and Special Programs Administration for the Safety and Security Review of Waterfront Import/Export Liquefied Natural Gas Facilities (Feb. 10, 2004), available at: https://www.phmsa.dot.gov/sites/phmsa.dot.gov/files/docs/InteragencyAgreemen
